titleText.es: ¿Sabes lo que ayuda mucho contra las crisis existenciales? Preguntarse cuánto espacio hay que dejar en la estantería para una colección de Terry Pratchett.
titleText.en: You know what really helps an existential crisis? Wondering how much shelf space to leave for a Terry Pratchett collection.
titleText.noteEn: The official English title text is preserved exactly; the Spanish archive gives a direct translation of the same shelf-space joke.

regions.labelEs: ¡YA TENGO TODOS LOS LIBROS DE MUNDODISCO!

excludedUnits.rationale: Mundodisco is the retained proper title of Terry Pratchett's fictional setting, not general Spanish vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: EH. HACER UNA COLECCIÓN EN EL KINDLE ME PARECE SIN SENTIDO.

excludedUnits.rationale: Kindle is the retained English product name of Amazon's e-reader, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Sin and sentido work together as the fixed description for something that lacks a reasonable point.
Parece reports the speaker's impression, and sin sentido supplies the description rather than asserting it as a fact.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, YA SÉ QUE EL DRM HARÁ QUE LOS PIERDA EN ALGÚN MOMENTO.

excludedUnits.rationale: DRM is the unchanged English technical acronym for digital rights management, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Hará que introduces a future caused result, while pierda is the special form of perder used for that caused action; los is the visible object of pierda.
Los stands before the changed verb pierda and replaces the masculine plural things that may be lost.
En algún momento leaves the future time deliberately unspecified.
Sin sentido gives the fixed description for something regarded as pointless.
En general broadens the judgment beyond one specific technical problem.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, HACIENDO COLECCIONES SATISFACES TUS IMPULSOS DE URRACA, PERO AÚN ASÍ ACABAS MURIENDO SOLO.

applications.explanationEn: Haciendo is the -iendo form that presents making collections as the means by which the following result occurs.
Aún así introduces a result that remains true despite the satisfaction just mentioned; this follows the source's accented spelling.
Acabas changes for one familiar listener, and muriendo names the eventual action using its -iendo form.

regions.labelEs: PERDÓN, A VECES CONFUNDO TUS CRISIS EXISTENCIALES CON PERSPICACIA TÉCNICA.

applications.explanationEn: A veces forms the fixed expression for something that happens sometimes.

applications.exampleEs: CONFUNDO TUS CRISIS EXISTENCIALES CON PERSPICACIA TÉCNICA
applications.explanationEn: Confundo names the mix-up, tus crisis existenciales fills the first complete item, con introduces the comparison, and perspicacia técnica fills the second complete item.
Crisis names the things first, and existenciales follows to describe their kind.
Existenciales uses its plural form to match the plural meaning of crisis.
Perspicacia names the quality first, and técnica follows to describe its domain.
Técnica uses feminine singular -a to match the feminine singular noun perspicacia.

regions.labelEs: YO A VECES CONFUNDO ESTO CON UN UNIVERSO AL QUE LE IMPORTO.

applications.explanationEn: A veces forms the fixed expression for something that happens sometimes.
Confundo names the mix-up, esto fills the first item, con introduces the comparison, and un universo fills the second item.
Al combines a with el before relative que, referring back to the masculine singular noun universo.
Le identifies the universe as the entity that cares, while importo agrees with the first-person thing that matters.

cards.noteEn: Libros is the masculine plural of libro.
A hesitation sound used while the speaker pauses to think or find words. This is different from eh used to call for attention or ask for agreement.
Hacer can mean creating or producing a physical thing. This is distinct from its very common sense “to do.”

example.en: We are going to make a table.

cards.answerEn: collection; a gathered set of related things
cards.noteEn: Colección is a feminine noun, so it uses una or la.

cards.answerEn: the; often omitted in English before a named item
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use el before the name or number of a masculine item, product, command, system, or service. An ordinary noun such as modelo or número may be understood rather than written. English often uses the name alone. El here is not accented él, 'he.'

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something seems to have a quality or state?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of parecer followed by the describing word.
cards.noteEn: The description agrees with the person or thing: parece cansado, parece cansada, parecen cansados. This reports an impression rather than asserting the state as a fact.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is pointless or meaningless?
cards.noteEn: The same expression can describe an action, statement, plan, or situation that lacks meaning or a reasonable point.
In sin sentido, it describes something with no meaning or point.

cards.answerEn: already; by now, often yet in a question
cards.noteEn: Ya marks that an expected action or state has been reached by the time being discussed. English usually says 'already' in a statement, but often 'yet' in a question about whether it has happened.

cards.answerEn: that; links an expression to its content or an outcome
cards.noteEn: Que can introduce what someone thinks, says, wants, causes, or allows, or what an evaluation is about. English may use 'that,' omit it, or reorganize the sentence with 'to' or 'for.' Que stays unaccented; the following verb form depends on the surrounding expression.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Hará is the future form of hacer for one person or thing.

example.es: El cambio hará que trabajemos mejor.
example.en: The change will make us work better.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone makes or gets another person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of hacer, then que, then the person and the action in a special caused-action form.
cards.noteEn: Hacer changes for who causes the action. The later verb uses a special form called the subjunctive because that action is being caused rather than simply reported: llama becomes llame, and cierra becomes cierre.

example.es: Hago que Ana cierre la puerta.
example.en: I make Ana close the door.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

cards.answerEn: I lose; I may lose (special form used for a caused or uncertain action)
cards.noteEn: Pierda is a special form of perder. The surrounding words identify who loses something.

example.es: No quiero que pierda las llaves.
example.en: I do not want her to lose the keys.

cards.answerEn: at; begins en algún momento, “at some point”
cards.noteEn: Here en introduces an indefinite point in time rather than a physical location.

example.en: We will discuss it at some point.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “at some point” without specifying when?
cards.noteEn: Algún comes before the masculine noun momento; the expression can refer to the past or future according to the verb.

example.en: We will see each other at some point.

cards.noteEn: Alguno loses its final o directly before a noun for one thing that uses el, such as libro: alguno becomes algún libro. This shortened form keeps its stress on the final syllable, written with an accent on ú. It does not identify which particular person or thing.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en general, “in general”
cards.noteEn: The two words form a fixed expression about an overall view.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce an overall view rather than one specific case?
cards.noteEn: It can appear at the beginning or end of a statement and means “in general” or “overall.”

example.es: La ciudad es tranquila en general.

cards.noteEn: The complete expression en general means “in general” or “overall.”

Haciendo is the unchanged -iendo action form of hacer, “to do or make.” With a form of estar, it describes an action in progress. Without estar, it can describe how another action happens or an activity happening at the same time. The surrounding construction supplies meanings such as English “by.”

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar followed by the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

cards.answerEn: collections; gathered sets of related things
cards.noteEn: This is the plural of colección.

cards.answerEn: you satisfy; you fulfill (one familiar person)
cards.noteEn: Satisfaces is the present form of satisfacer used with tú.

example.es: Con ese trabajo satisfaces tu curiosidad.
example.en: With that work, you satisfy your curiosity.

cards.noteEn: It refers to strong sudden desires or tendencies.

example.en: He controlled his urges to buy things.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to its type, purpose, or field
cards.noteEn: Spanish often puts de between two nouns where English puts the describing noun first. In una silla de oficina, oficina tells you the chair's intended use. This is different from de naming an owner, material, contents, or a part's larger whole.
A urraca is a black-and-white bird popularly associated with collecting shiny objects.

example.es: Una urraca se posó en la rama.
example.en: A magpie landed on the branch.

cards.noteEn: In this contrast expression, aun is now commonly written without an accent, although the printed source uses aún.

example.en: It was late; even so, we continued.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “even so” or “nevertheless”?
cards.answerEn: Use aun así; the spelling aún así is also widespread.
cards.noteEn: The expression introduces something that remains true despite the preceding difficulty or contrast. Current standard spelling normally omits the accent when aun means “even.”

example.en: She was tired; even so, she finished.

cards.noteEn: Together, aun así introduces a result that remains true despite the previous point.

example.en: It was raining; even so, we went out.

cards.noteEn: Here acabar describes the eventual result, not simply finishing an object.

example.en: If you do not ask, you end up waiting.

cards.promptEs: acabar seguido de una acción en -ando o -iendo
cards.questionEn: How do you use acabar to say that someone ends up doing something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of acabar followed by the action in its -ando or -iendo form.
cards.noteEn: Only acabar changes for the person and time: acaba hablando, acabaron hablando. The second form names the eventual action, which may be unintended. This form is called a gerund: hablar becomes hablando, comer becomes comiendo, and some verbs change their stem, as morir becomes muriendo. Do not add de: acabar de hablar means having just spoken, a different pattern.

example.en: After arguing, we ended up laughing.

cards.noteEn: Muriendo is the irregular -iendo form of morir.
When solo describes a masculine person's state, it means alone or lonely rather than “only.” The feminine form is sola.

example.es: Se sintió solo en la ciudad nueva.
example.en: He felt lonely in the new city.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.
In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

cards.answerEn: I confuse; I mistake one thing for another
cards.noteEn: Use con before the second thing in confundo X con Y.

example.es: A veces confundo la sal con el azúcar.
example.en: Sometimes I mistake salt for sugar.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone mistakes one thing for another?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of confundir, name the first thing, add con, then name the second thing.
cards.noteEn: Confundir changes for the person and time, but con remains unchanged between the two people or things being mixed up.

example.es: Confundieron la entrada con la salida.
example.en: They mistook the entrance for the exit.

cards.noteEn: The written form crisis is the same in singular and plural; nearby words reveal the number.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: It describes questions or crises about existence, meaning, or purpose.

cards.answerEn: with; introduces the second thing in a mix-up
cards.noteEn: The pattern is confundir X con Y: to confuse or mistake X for Y.

example.es: Confundí su abrigo con el mío.
example.en: I mistook her coat for mine.

cards.noteEn: It is the ability to notice and understand things clearly.
The ending -a matches a feminine singular noun such as perspicacia.
Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.
Al combines a and el into one word. Spanish requires this combined form when the two occur together.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: marks one person or entity as the one having a feeling, preference, or impression
cards.noteEn: Le can identify him, her, formal you, or another singular person or entity experiencing a reaction. What causes the reaction controls the verb: le gusta el libro, but le gustan los libros. Le stays the same; a phrase such as a Ana can clarify who it refers to.

example.es: A Ana le gustan los trenes.

cards.promptEs: importar con la persona a quien le importa
cards.questionEn: How do you use importar to say what matters and who cares about it?
cards.answerEn: Make importar match the thing or person that matters; use me, te, le, nos, os, or les to say who cares.
cards.noteEn: For one thing or a whole situation, use importa; for several things, use importan: me importa el precio, me importan los detalles. The short word names who cares: me is to me, te to familiar singular you, le to him/her/formal singular you, nos to us, os to familiar plural you mainly in Spain, and les to them or plural you with ustedes. Ustedes is the usual plural you in Latin America and formal plural you in most of Spain. If I am the person who matters, use importo, as in le importo ('I matter to him or her'). You can omit the person when it is not needed: importa el resultado. No makes it negative and goes before the short word, if present: no me importa.

cards.answerEn: I matter; I am important to someone
cards.noteEn: Importo is the first-person singular form of importar in the sense of mattering.

example.es: Sé que importo a mis amigos.
example.en: I know that I matter to my friends.
